findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T12] Unaudited privilege-escalation chain: manage_permissions → remote_access
findings.detail: manage_permissions lets any caller (unauthenticated, per pre_auth_injection finding) grant arbitrary 'permission' strings to arbitrary 'user' on arbitrary 'resource' with no validation, ownership check, or approval workflow. Because remote_access treats 'auth_token' as merely optional, an attacker can first call manage_permissions to self-grant an admin/privileged permission record (even if the backend doesn't strictly enforce it, many downstream systems key authorization off exactly this kind of permission table), then call remote_access against 'database' or 'fileserver' using the newly granted context. This two-tool chain was not captured by the existing attack_chain findings (which only pair remote_access with itself) and represents a distinct privilege-escalation-then-exfiltration path.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T02] Authorization bypass by design: auth_token is optional on a privileged command-execution tool
findings.detail: The schema marks 'auth_token' as optional (default null) while the description states it is required only for 'privileged operations.' This implies remote_access will execute attacker-supplied commands on named backend systems even with no token at all — i.e., the tool's own contract admits that unauthenticated command execution is a supported, intended path, not merely a theft target. This is a distinct issue from the reported token_theft finding: the risk isn't just that a token could be stolen, it's that the tool functions perfectly well without one, meaning 'privileged' is not actually enforced server-side.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T22] manage_permissions 'permission' parameter lacks enum/allow-list validation
findings.detail: The docstring implies only 'grant' or 'revoke' are valid values for 'permission', but the schema accepts any unbounded string. This allows malformed or injected values (e.g. multi-value strings, delimiters, or payloads intended for a downstream permission-parsing engine) to be passed through unchecked, which is a schema design flaw distinct from the already-reported unbounded-string findings — the missing constraint is semantic (business-logic enum), not just length.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T31] 'system' parameter functions as an unrestricted internal target selector (lateral movement / SSRF-like primitive)
findings.detail: Beyond enabling command injection (already flagged), the 'system' argument itself is a free-text pointer to internal infrastructure ('database', 'webserver', 'fileserver'). Combined with no allow-list, this turns remote_access into a generic internal-network pivot primitive: an attacker with any access to this tool can address arbitrary named internal hosts/services, independent of the command-injection payload mechanics. This is a network-boundary/lateral-movement issue, not merely a command-injection issue, and should be tracked separately from the semicolon_chain finding.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T41] Unbounded 'result' output field creates a staging channel for bulk exfiltration or secondary injection
findings.detail: outputSchema for both tools defines 'result' as an unbounded string with no length cap or content sanitization. Given remote_access's demonstrated exfiltration_url leakage and command execution capability, this output channel can carry arbitrarily large data back through the MCP transport (bulk data staging) or return attacker-crafted text designed to re-inject instructions into the calling LLM session on subsequent turns. This is distinct from the already-reported tool_response_injection finding, which focuses on reflection of the 'system' input rather than the absence of output constraints.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T44] Disagreement: native_function_identity_erasure should be rated higher than MEDIUM given the toolset's capabilities
findings.detail: The deterministic scan rates 'No caller identity in tool calls' as MEDIUM. Given that this server exposes both an unauthenticated shell/database/secrets execution primitive (remote_access) and an unauthenticated permission-management primitive (manage_permissions) in the same pre-auth surface, the absence of caller identity is not a moderate hygiene gap — it removes any possibility of attributing who executed commands or who granted/revoked permissions on sensitive systems. Combined with the CRITICAL excessive_permissions and CRITICAL command_injection findings already reported, this identity gap should be elevated to HIGH: it is a force-multiplier for every other finding on this server, not an independent, lower-severity issue.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T12] No cross-tool consistency check between manage_permissions grants and remote_access enforcement
findings.detail: There is no evidence the server actually consults permissions set via manage_permissions when remote_access is invoked (no shared 'resource'/'system' correlation in the schemas). This means manage_permissions may create a false sense of access control while providing no real gate on remote_access, misleading an operator or downstream automation into believing least-privilege is enforced when it is not — a governance/traceability gap that compounds the excessive_permissions findings already reported.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T08] Unsolicited disclosure of privileged system name (tool 'remote_access')
findings.detail: The error response reveals 'admin-console' as an available remote system, which was not mentioned in the tool's documented examples (database, webserver, fileserver). This unsolicited enumeration could encourage the LLM or user to target a privileged/administrative endpoint that may not have been intended for exposure, potentially aiding reconnaissance for further exploitation.

findings.title: [AI] [MCP-T05] Unauthenticated privilege escalation via manage_permissions chained into remote_access RCE
findings.detail: 1) Attacker connects with no credentials (finding: 'Unauthenticated MCP initialize accepted' / 'Pre-auth tool access: 2 tools available without authentication'). 2) Attacker calls manage_permissions(user='attacker', resource='admin-console', permission='grant') — the tool has no auth_token param and no identity binding (native_function_identity_erasure), so the grant succeeds with no authorization check. 3) Attacker then calls remote_access(system='admin-console', command='<payload>', auth_token='') using the resource name granted in step 2 as the 'system' value; the confirmed command-injection primitive (semicolon_chain, evidence: 'test; echo MCPNUKE_T05_SEMICOLON') lets the attacker execute arbitrary shell commands on the now-'authorized' admin-console target. The scanner flagged manage_permissions only for schema issues and never connected it to remote_access despite it being the actual privilege-escalation gate.
